title: The FDA Just Said There's 'Little Evidence' Behind the Peptides Millions of Americans Are Injecting
excerpt: BPC-157, TB-500, and five other peptides popular in wellness circles face a July FDA review — while the advisory panel itself includes sellers and promoters of the same compounds.
body:
If you've scrolled through health and wellness content on Instagram or TikTok in the past year, you've almost certainly encountered peptides. Short chains of amino acids marketed as everything from gut healers and joint fixers to fat burners and anti-aging elixirs, these compounds have become the hottest trend in the biohacking and longevity space — despite one critical problem: there is almost no evidence they work in humans.

On Monday, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) released staff review documents ahead of a July 23-24 meeting of its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee. The verdict from FDA reviewers was blunt: available evidence does not support allowing compounding pharmacies to manufacture seven of the most popular peptides, and the lack of adequate human trials means their safety profiles remain largely unknown.

The Seven Peptides Under Review

The peptides heading for the committee include some of the biggest names in the wellness underground:

  • **BPC-157** — promoted for gut healing and ulcerative colitis, with a devoted online following but only animal studies to back the claims
  • **TB-500** — marketed for wound healing and injury recovery, popular among athletes
  • **KPV** — touted for wound healing and anti-inflammatory effects
  • **MOTS-c** — sold for obesity treatment and osteoporosis
  • **Emideltide** — promoted for opioid withdrawal and chronic insomnia
  • **Semax** — claimed to help with migraines, chronic pain, and cerebral ischemia
  • **Epitalon** — marketed for insomnia and anti-aging

FDA staff reviewers highlighted that evidence supporting these peptides' effectiveness "is scant" and flagged "risks related to immunogenicity, toxicity and impurity." In 2023, the Biden administration had barred compounding pharmacies from manufacturing peptides for the same reasons.

> "A major *Nature* feature published this week — "Is the peptide craze backed by science?" — explored the gap between peptide marketing and evidence."

The Panel Controversy

What makes this review particularly fraught is the composition of the advisory panel itself. According to CNN, the committee includes more than a half-dozen panelists who run clinics, online businesses, or pharmacies that specialize in selling peptides — the very compounds they are being asked to evaluate.

One panelist runs clinics in Florida selling peptide injections, testosterone, and weight-loss medications as part of a national chain. Another charges $500 for "peptide and hormone" consultations and promotes BPC-157 to thousands of followers on social media, with a disclaimer that each consultation "is educational in nature and does not constitute medical care." A third is a Tennessee state senator whose family pharmacy sells compounded medications for weight loss and longevity.

The committee's recommendations are non-binding, but they will inform the FDA's final decision on whether these compounds can legally be manufactured and sold by compounding pharmacies.

What Does the Science Actually Say?

A major *Nature* feature published this week — "Is the peptide craze backed by science?" — explored the gap between peptide marketing and evidence. The conclusion: animal research suggests some of these molecules hold genuine therapeutic promise, but the leap from rat studies to human medicine hasn't been made.

The distinction matters. BPC-157, for instance, has shown remarkable wound-healing effects in rodent models. But no large, randomized, controlled trial in humans has been published. The doses, delivery methods, purity, and long-term safety profiles that would normally be established before a drug reaches patients simply don't exist for most of these compounds.

Meanwhile, legitimate peptide research continues to advance through proper channels. A University of Alberta team recently published results in *Cell Biomaterials* showing that a human-derived antimicrobial peptide, D-GK17, can destroy bacterial biofilms — the sticky matrices that make many infections resistant to antibiotics. That work followed the rigorous preclinical pipeline that the wellness peptides have bypassed.

Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

The peptide trend has found a receptive audience among health-conscious Indian Americans, as well as the broader Indian diaspora in the UK and Canada. Diaspora communities that embrace Ayurvedic and functional medicine traditions are often early adopters of novel wellness therapies — and the marketing for peptides deliberately targets this demographic with language about "natural" healing and "cellular repair."

The compounds are readily available through compounding pharmacies, telehealth consultations, and online wellness platforms across the United States, UK, and Canada. Many are administered via self-injection, with dosing guidance sourced from social media influencers rather than clinical trials.

For South Asians with a family history of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or autoimmune conditions — populations that might be especially drawn to peptides promising metabolic or anti-inflammatory benefits — the FDA's message is worth heeding: the absence of evidence of harm is not evidence of safety. Until proper human trials are conducted, these compounds remain experimental in the truest sense of the word. This caution is particularly relevant for NRIs who may be seeking alternative health solutions and could be influenced by online trends without sufficient scientific backing.

*Sources: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Reuters, Nature, CNN, Cell Biomaterials*
